doc.title: Rudy Van Gelder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Pro Tools, Photoshop and the loss of belief in the real thing
summary: He never liked Pro Tools, and compares editing in Photoshop and in layered recordings to eroding trust in the real performance.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I asked Maureen about this. She mentioned that you’re always looking at the latest technology that comes in and I asked a question about Pro Tools. That’s something that you ventured into, dabbled into a little bit?

Pro Tools became the de facto standard for editing. But frankly, I never liked it. I never used it. There is something about it that’s negative to me. I have a system that I used that’s very comfortable. In two areas, both systems I have are comfortable in two areas. On neither Pro Tools nor… I mean understand me I am heavy into editing and still
getting better at that too. But Pro Tools is not the answer for me. What did you say when you walked in here and saw my pictures?
I, because I absolutely love photographs, I was absolutely quite stunned by the images of the birds.
That’s not what you said. Tell me what you said.
Cause I know I would have to, to be able to capture a shot like that.
You see how deep that is? It actually destroys your belief in photography.

Well, it goes back to what you’re talking about, the whole idea of being able to lay tracks and go back. So you don’t know what you’re really getting. When you go out and you find yourself paying $100 or so to see this artist live, you realized, “Wait a minute.”
That’s exactly what I mean. That’s exactly the same thing.
